title: The Woman Who Killed Marat: Why the Court Would Not Believe She Acted Alone
dek: Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone. The revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.
why: High information density, tracing a causal chain from the institutional origins of the Terror through paper-money inflation to the Vendée war, with the assassination details in the second half especially valuable.
who: Listeners interested in the French Revolution, the origins of the Terror, and the mechanics of political violence; readers who want to understand how populist language and revolutionary institutions get improvised.
skip: The last two minutes are a trailer for another podcast, with no historical content, and can be skipped.

points.h: The assassination declaration was written before the act
points.body: When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile of villains," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and is therefore outside the law," and called on the French to "rise. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc defense; it was written before the act — what she wanted was not escape but to turn her death into a rallying point.

points.h: Marat was the first modern populist
points.body: Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His formula included: constantly invoking the capitalized "People," claiming the people are at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theory, openly stating that his goal was to keep readers "perpetually alert," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests, and the like. The show points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used by both left and right today.

points.h: Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
points.body: In early 1793 France suffered successive poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government, lacking money for war, could only print paper money, the assignat, with about four billion in circulation. This caused severe inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, protests occurred almost daily in the markets, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The show stresses: these were the very same conditions that had sparked the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "The Revolution happened, yet life has not improved, so someone must be scheming."

points.h: The commander's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
points.body: On March 8, 1793, the Austrians counterattacked and decisively defeated Dumouriez at Neerwinden, forcing him to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to emulate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, asking his subordinates, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On April 5 he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking with him a number of senior officers, including the future French king Louis Philippe. A volunteer wrote to his mother: "Whom can we trust now?"

The show stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint, no plan; they were built as they went along, only later appearing as a machine, and many who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On March 10 the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal, located in the Palais de Justice in Paris, with the existing Conciergerie prison in its basement. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

points.h: The Girondins used new rules to strike at Marat, and it backfired
points.body: Having just abolished parliamentary immunity, the Girondins, while many deputies were away on missions to the provinces, indicted Marat on April 14, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat first went into hiding for three days, then, finding that Parisian street opinion was on his side, turned himself in for trial. On April 24 the trial opened at the Palais de Justice; the chief prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard supporter and allowed Marat a long self-defense. The ten-man jury acquitted him within hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by some 800 people, wearing a crown of roses, with cries of "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a complete humiliation.

points.h: Corday buys a knife: a 15-centimeter black-handled kitchen knife
points.body: Around eight in the morning on July 13, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the Palais-Royal arcades, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing her white Norman-style hat. She entered a cutlery shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 centimeters long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but, lacking an appointment, was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

points.h: The court would not believe a woman could act alone
points.body: Corday was arrested on the spot; one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognized Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: it is impossible, because you say Marat is the source of all France's ills, yet Marat is precisely the one who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators, so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you are mad; only in Paris do people see Marat, in the provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that provincials would think Marat a bad man.
